title: Declare your faith (Shahada)
whyMatters: Taking the Shahada is how you formally enter Islam. It is the one step everything else rests on: a declaration that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is His messenger. Saying it wipes away what came before and hands you a clean slate. Ask around and you will find plenty of Muslims who remember the moment they said it more clearly than almost anything else.

exactActions.text: Know what the words actually say
subSteps: The Shahada means: 'I bear witness that there is no deity except Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.'
Sit with that for a minute and think about what it means for you.

exactActions.text: Learn how it sounds in Arabic
subSteps: 'Ash-hadu an la ilaha ill-Allah, wa ash-hadu anna Muhammadan rasul-Allah'
Listen to a recording if you can find one. Your pronunciation does not have to be perfect.
You can say it alone at home or with witnesses at a masjid.
What counts is that you mean it, not where you happen to be standing.
If you would like a small ceremony, many masjids are glad to arrange one.
You are Muslim now. Let that land.
Make a simple du'a (prayer) and ask Allah to guide you.
If there is someone you trust, this is worth telling them.

obstacles.solution: Your pronunciation does not have to be perfect. Allah knows what you meant. Arabic speakers had to learn these words too. Listen to a recording and practice if it helps, but meaning it matters more than getting every sound right.

If you believe in your heart that there is one God and that Muhammad is His messenger, you are ready. Feeling nervous is normal. You do not have to know everything about Islam first, because that part comes after. If you are still thinking it over, there is no deadline. The page "Thinking about Islam?", linked below, is written for you.

obstacles.problem: I don't have anyone to witness it
obstacles.solution: Said sincerely, the Shahada counts even if you are alone in a room. Having it witnessed at a masjid does give you community support and a record, and you can arrange that later whenever you want to.

Almost every convert worries about this. You do not have to announce it to everyone right away. Take your time and tell people when you are ready. There is help available for the family conversations when you get to them.

tinyVersion: If this feels like too much, say it in your own words for now: 'I believe there is only one God and Muhammad is His messenger.' The formal Arabic can come later.
unlocksNext: Now that you have declared your faith, you are ready to learn the full-body wash (Ghusl) and start your life as a Muslim.

contextNotes.title: Private, at a masjid, or online: your choice
contextNotes.body: Said sincerely, the Shahada counts wherever you say it. Ustadha Shireen Ahmed (SeekersGuidance) writes that she has heard it is better said in front of others, even just a few people, but that it is not strictly necessary if it makes you anxious. Take that as a suggestion, not a rule. The reason for others knowing is practical: your community knows you are Muslim, for example when it comes to a marriage or a Muslim burial.

contextNotes.title: Saying it at a masjid
contextNotes.body: Phone the masjid office and ask for a quiet Shahada with the imam and one or two people. Ask whether they give a certificate and what they need from you. If you do not want photos or videos, say so before you arrive. Nobody should record your Shahada or post it online without your clear permission, and you can say no on the day.

contextNotes.title: Saying it online or on a video call
contextNotes.body: A SeekersGuidance answer by Shaykh Abdurragmaan Khan says a Shahada said through an online service is valid. Saying it again with a local imam is not required, though the answer calls it "undoubtedly desired". It also advises you to connect with a local community and introduce yourself to one of its leaders. This is one scholar's answer, so ask a local imam if you are unsure.

contextNotes.title: Your own words or the Arabic
contextNotes.body: Imam Yama Niazi (SeekersGuidance) says it is more cautious to include "ashhadu" (I bear witness), and that the Shahada is also acceptable without it. If you first said it in your own words, you can say the Arabic form later. There is no need to keep repeating it out of worry.
